Partial match: tgt=9 changes some comps. But which target? In demo6, changed comp became 8 not 9. And many other cells changed... maybe recolor should be per-twin pair: each duplicate shape gets recolored to the color of the unique singleton of that shape? Demo6: bar1@(0,17) and bar2@(4,16) same sig. One becomes 8. The 8 comp is large blob at top. Maybe rule: for each duplicated-shape pair with same color, the copy farther from... hmm. Or: the twin pair, one matches a third comp of different color (like in demos 2-5 partial). Actually output demo6 col values: comps list [5,6,6,6,6,6,8,8,9,9,9] — after change bars became 8? No, both are still 6? The changed comp box (4,16)-(4,20) remains 6 per go listing... wait earlier go listing showed comps colors unchanged. So change was row0 cols17-21 becoming 8. That's bar(0,17) → 8! Bar(0,17) shape = 1x5 horizontal; does any other color have 1x5? Yes, part of 9 comp? Hmm.

Maybe rule: each shape appears exactly once in the output except shapes that appear twice get... Actually simpler: maybe the two identical bars are "noise": one stays, other must become the color of another object whose bounding box contains it? 8-comp spans rows0-2 cols15-21 — includes row0 col17-21 region but not the cell (0,17)? yes (0,17),(0,18),(0,19),(0,20),(0,21) all inside 8 comp bbox. Also (4,16) bar not in 8's bbox (rows 0-2). So rule: recolor the duplicate whose bounding box overlaps the big unique comp to that comp's color! Test on demo1: changed 9@(16,1)-(20,9) size33 twin with 9@(0,0) size33 same sig. Which one is in... 5-comp bbox? The 5 comp is (0,0)-(6,10). Not overlapping either. Hmm, but also 5 has other comps? demo1 5 comps: only one (17 cells). Overlap with (0,0)? no. Overlap with (16,1)? no. Doesn't work.

Alternative: overlap between the duplicate and a DIFFERENT-color comp that shares its shape pattern? 5 comp shape: let me just test programmatically: for each pair of equal-sig comps (any colors), if one overlaps another comp of a different color, recolor to that color. Check demo1: the 9@(16,1)-(20,9) overlaps 6 comp? Its bbox rows16-20 cols1-9... 6 comps near: (14,19) small... no. Hmm.

Better: compute what actually changed in each demo: diff positions. Then infer.

Changed cells always a subset of a whole object recolored to another color. Demo 5: single cell 0→3 (singletons!). Demo 1: 9@(16,4)... wait changed region is rows16-20 cols1-9 = the big 9 comp (16,1)-(20,9), recolored to 5. Earlier I noted it. But also note demo1 has two 9 comps both size 33 with SAME shape; the changed one got color 5 while the other stayed 9? Output row0 shows 9 at top-left and row16+ shows 5. So rule isn't "recolor duplicates". Let me reconsider: maybe each object gets recolored based on... In demo 1, changed object's new color 5. What's special about it? It's the lower copy. Top-left 9 stays. Hmm.

Demo 2: object 2 at (17..19,8) → 9. Colors present: many. Maybe rule: recolor objects so that each color appears exactly once per shape? Like each distinct shape should have one color? Actually check: in demo1 there are two identical-shape objects both color 9; output makes them different colors — one 9, one 5. That means rule: shapes duplicated within same color get split/renamed? No—only one changed.

Demo 4: object 4@(9,12)-(11,17) → 1. Is there a twin? Comp 4 (0,0)-(2,5) area 13 sig same! Yes earlier twins exist. And target color 1 — is 1 singleton? yes 1 comp only. In demo6: bar 6@(4,16)-(4,20) → 8. Twin: 6@(0,17)-(0,21) bar same color! Also 8 comp exists (singleton). Hmm but why did (0,17) bar stay 6? Because the rule picks which twin changes — maybe the one NOT touching something? Or the one closer/farther from target-color object?

Wait — maybe rule is: when two identical shapes have same color, they must be distinguished: the one nearer to / overlapping with something gets color X. In demo6, the lower one becomes 8? no, upper stayed. Changed one is (4,16) lower. Why 8? Maybe color = color of nearest other component? Check demo2: object 2 at (17..3,8)? changed cells (17-19,8): vertical line of 3 → what is it near? Probably adjacent to 9 somewhere. Need data.

Actually maybe simpler: rule could be "recolor to match the shape-duplicate pair partner": the twin of changed comp has color X? But twin here is same color 6 in demo6. Hmm.

Let me just compute: for each changed object, find what determines new color: e.g., which object shares its exact bounding box relationship or its position (second occurrence).

Wait, but only some cells changed? The changed region covers cols 2-9... but the whole component should be recolored. No—the bug: for o in vs, if dups exists, we recolor. But the True/Falses show partial. In demo1, comp 9@(16,1) has a twin comp 9@(0,0) same sig. My loop over both — when processing first, dups found, recolor. When processing second, dups = [first], also recolor. Should work. But result shows mismatch... maybe because `go` is recomputed each call? go=np.array(gi) fine. Mismatches: rows 2-7 etc. Those correspond to other comps. Demo1 mismatches include col21ish regions where my f didn't change but expected did. Likely rule: not just within-same-color duplicates; any two comps with identical shape regardless of color get one recolored to target color (the largest unique comp). Let me test: recolor all comps whose shape appears elsewhere (any color), except keep one instance. Which instance changes? Perhaps the one farther from origin / smaller? Test variants quickly.

But budget: I've used many turns. Better run one careful script testing multiple rule variants against all demos, then decide.

import numpy as np
# In all demos only ONE comp changes color. Identify which comp is the changed one: the comp whose shape duplicates a comp of the TARGET color?
# Demo6: changed bar 6@(4,16)-(4,20); target 8 (the big 9-cell blob). Is there an 8-shaped twin? no.
# Maybe rule: recolor comp that has SAME SHAPE as another comp of the same color but different... let's check per demo the changed comp's sig and which other comps share it EXACTLY (incl same color), plus target color identity.
for i in range(1,7):
    name=f'Demo pair {i}'
    gi=np.array(G[name+' input']); go=np.array(G[name+' output'])
    ch=[o for o in comps(gi) if not np.array_equal(gi[o['box'][0]:o['box'][2]+1,o['box'][1]:o['box'][3]+1],go[o['box'][0]:o['box'][2]+1,o['box'][1]:o['box'][3]+1])][0]
    print(name,'changed comp:',ch['c'],ch['area'],'sig size',len(ch['sub']))
    same_color_same_sig=[d for d in comps(gi) if d['c']==ch['c'] and d['sub']==ch['sub']]
    print('  same-color-twins:',[(d['area'],d['box']) for d in same_color_same_sig],'count',len(same_color_same_sig))

steps.text:
Interesting! In every demo, the changed comp has exactly 2 same-color twins of identical shape (same color & sig). So: find comps where same-color duplicates exist; recolor one of them. But which one and to what color?

- D1: 9@(16,1) changed to 5. Other twin 9@(0,0) kept. 5 is the singleton color (one comp of 5).
- D4: 4@(9,12) changed to 1. 1 is a singleton color (one comp). The other twin 4@(0,0) kept.
- D6: 6@(4,16) changed to 8. But 8... in D6 there's one 8 comp (big blob) and it's not duplicate. Hmm but 8 appears once as a component — so target = color of a singleton component? But wait, in D6, the two 6 bars are twins and one becomes 8. Why 8? Maybe the rule is different: the twin pair should become... Actually maybe rule: each duplicated shape must be recolored so that only one copy per color-shape exists; the "extra" copies get recolored to the color of another object whose shape matches? Hmm.

Wait D2: changed 2@(17,8)-(19,8), vertical 3-cell line; twin 2@(17,8)... no—changed IS the one at (17,8); its twin? same-color-twins count 1 means only the changed itself? It lists [(3,(17,8),(19,8))] which includes itself. Hmm.

Actually maybe the true rule: shapes appearing multiple times within same color must all be unified to ONE instance, with extra copies recolored to... hmm. Let me think about what determines target color:
- D1: target 5 (singleton comp of 5, 17 cells). Changed comp 9@16 size 33.
- D4: target 1 (comp of 1, 12 cells at top-left, big). Changed 4@(9,12) size 13.
- D5: target 3; 0 singletons: changed 0@(9,2)? earlier changed was single cell? D5 change cells [[9,2]] one cell. Hmm changed comp '0' single cell at (9,2)? Its twins: two single 0 cells elsewhere plus itself → three twins. Target 3.

Maybe rule: recolor duplicates of the TARGET shape to target color. I.e., some color X has ONE comp whose shape is duplicated by many other comps; those duplicates are recolored to... no, they're recolored to X.

Alternative reading: the comp that changes is one whose shape is DUPLICATED elsewhere, and after change that shape will have unique... Actually simplest: the rule might be "recolor ALL comps whose shape occurs more than once (in any color?) to the color of ..." hmm.

Look again: D2 changed 2@(17,8) vertical bar; does any other color have a vertical 3-line? Probably yes! And D3 changed 5@(12,17) an L/shape; D5 changed 0@(9,2); D6 changed 6@(4,16).

Hypothesis: the grid contains pairs of same-shaped objects in DIFFERENT colors. One of each pair is the "template". All extra copies of that template shape are recolored to the template's color? No—the changed ones become a NEW color equal to something else present.

Actually simpler hypothesis matching data: For each color C, if it has ≥2 components sharing the same shape (a duplicate pair within color), one copy gets recolored to the color of the LARGEST singleton component? D1: largest singleton = 5 comp(17 cells). ✓. D4: largest singleton = 1 (12 cells vs others?). Check: D4 comps: colors 1(12,big comp), 3 x2 singles, 4 two dupes, 5 x2, 6 single, 7 x2. Singleton colors: 3(2 cells? area1 each ×2 comps—those are separate comps so color 3 has TWO comps → not singleton). Singleton colors in D4: 6 (one comp), 1 (one comp), 5? 5 has two comps. So singleton colors = {1,6}. Largest = 1. ✓ target 1!

D1: colors counts: 4 bg, 5 one comp → singleton. 6: many comps. 9: two dupes + small ones. 5 is the only singleton color? then target=5. ✓

D5: check singleton colors: 3 likely one comp; changed 0 has 3+ singles (dups within 0). Also 3 may appear once. Target 3 ✓ plausible.

D6: singleton colors: 5 (one comp of 2 cells), 8 (one comp of 9 cells), 9? 9 has 3 comps. 6 many. So singleton colors = {5,8}. Largest = 8. ✓ target 8!

def solve(gi):
    gi=np.array(gi)
    bg=int(np.bincount(gi.flatten()).argmax())
    cs=comps_nogb(gi,bg)

    for o in cs: cnt_by_color[o['c']]+=1
    tg=[c for c,n in cnt_by_color.items() if n==1][0]
    tgt=[o for o in cs if o['c']==tg][0]
    cnts=defaultdict(list)
    for o in cs: cnts[o['sub']].append(o)
    dupes={s:v for s,v in cnts.items() if len(v)>1 and v[0]['area']>1}
    # prefer pair whose shape == target shape; else any twin pair; recolor farther member(s)
    out=gi.copy()

    # score: prefer twins matching target shape, then more members
    scored=sorted(pairs,key=lambda p:(p[0],-p[1]))
    best=scored[0][3] if scored else None
    for o in dupes[best]:
        if mind(o,tgt)>mind(dupes[best][1-if 0 or 2]-1,tgt):
            pass
    return out
